title: Twenty-year follow-up of aerobic power and body composition of older track athletes
authors: Pollock ML, Mengelkoch LJ, Graves JE, Lowenthal DT, Limacher MC, Foster C, Wilmore JH
population: 21 older male-and-female track athletes followed 20 years (mean age 50.5 at baseline, 60.2 at 10 y, 70.4 at 20 y), grouped by training level: high (n=9), moderate (n=10), low (n=2)
findings: VO2max decreased at each testing point in all groups: high-intensity group 8% and 15%, moderate 13% and 14%, low (greatly reduced training) 18% and 34%, for T1 to T2 and T2 to T3 respectively.
Maximal heart rate decreased linearly by approximately 5-7 beats/min per decade and was independent of training status.

Body weight remained stable in high and moderate groups, percent fat increased about 2-2.5% per decade, fat-free weight decreased at each point with a trend for those who began weight training to better maintain it.

The authors conclude physiological capacities of older athletes are reduced despite continued vigorous endurance exercise over 20 years (approximately 8-15% per decade), with body-composition change less than in the sedentary population and related to training habits.
limitations: Very small, self-selected cohort, only 2 in the low-training group; 1970s-era athletes and testing; track athletes, not runners across distances; attrition.
implications: Even consistently training runners lose VO2max at roughly 8-15% per decade in the 50s-70s, so long-range targets should include decline; reduced or stopped training roughly doubles to triples the loss (low group 18% and 34%).
HRmax falls roughly 5-7 bpm per decade regardless of training status: recalibrate observed HRmax over time and do not expect training to hold it.
Supports including resistance training for masters to help maintain fat-free mass (trend only).
